```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(knitr)
library(tidymodels)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.asp = 0.56,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%",
  fig.retina = 3,
  fig.path = "./images/04-slr-f26/",
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE
)
options(width = 80, digits = 3)

theme_set(
  theme_classic(base_size = 18) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 16),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
)

mpg_data <- ggplot2::mpg |>
  filter(!is.na(displ), !is.na(hwy)) |>
  mutate(displ_c = displ - mean(displ))

fit_mpg <- lm(hwy ~ displ, data = mpg_data)
fit_mpg_c <- lm(hwy ~ displ_c, data = mpg_data)

new_car <- data.frame(displ = 3)
new_car_ci <- as.data.frame(predict(fit_mpg, newdata = new_car, interval = "confidence"))
new_car_pi <- as.data.frame(predict(fit_mpg, newdata = new_car, interval = "prediction"))

hook_output <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("output")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(output = function(x, options) {
  lines <- options$output.lines
  if (is.null(lines)) {
    return(hook_output(x, options))  # pass to default hook
  }
  x <- unlist(strsplit(x, "\n"))
  more <- "..."
  if (length(lines)==1) {        # first n lines
    if (length(x) > lines) {
      # truncate the output, but add ....
      x <- c(head(x, lines), more)
    }
  } else {
    x <- c(more, x[lines], more)
  }
  # paste these lines together
  x <- paste(c(x, ""), collapse = "\n")
  hook_output(x, options)
})
```

<!-- # Conditional Thinking -->

## Explore Conditional Relationships

<!-- ::: {.columns} -->
<!-- ::: {.column width="52%"} -->

Regression is a tool for making **conditional statements**:

> What should we expect for $Y$ when $X = x$?

. . .

::: alert

**Example.** *What highway miles per gallon (MPG) ($Y$) should we expect for a car with an engine displacement ($X$) of 3 liters?*

:::

We wanna learn **how $Y$ varies or changes with values of $X$**, not the other way around.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: midi

| $Y$ | $X$ |
|:---------:|:---------:|
| Response variable| Predictor |
| Outcome variable | Covariate |
| Dependent variable | Independent variable |
| Output variable | Input variable |
| Endogenous variable | Exogenous variable |
| Target variable | Explanatory variable |
| Label | Feature |
| Regressand | Regressor |
| ...  | ... |

:::

:::


::: {.column width="50%"}

::: fragment

::: midi

| Instead of Asking | Better to Ask |
|:--------------|:------------|
| Are $X$ and $Y$ related? | [How does $Y$ vary across values of $X$?]{.red} |

:::

:::

:::

::::

::: notes

Week 1 already introduced regression broadly. This slide narrows the focus: simple linear regression is about conditional thinking, not just drawing a line.

:::


<!-- ::: -->
<!-- ::: {.column width="48%"} -->
## {visibility="hidden"}


| Instead of Asking | Better to Ask |
|------------|------------|
| Are $X$ and $Y$ related? | How does $Y$ vary across values of $X$? |
| Is the slope significant? | Is the estimated change meaningful? |
| What is the best line? | Is a line useful for this question? |

<!-- ::: -->
<!-- ::: -->


##  (Linear) Regression Workflow

| Step | Question | Main tool |
|-----|----------|------|
| 1. Question | Prediction, description, comparison, or causal claim? | Context |
| 2. Data | What do the variables actually measure? | Scatterplot |
| 3. Fit | What line summarizes the pattern? | Least squares/Maximum likelihood |
| 4. Uncertainty | How stable is the fitted line? | Simulation / Intervals |
| 5. Prediction | Mean response or one new observation? | Prediction bands |
| 6. Check | What does the line miss? | Residuals / Sensitivity |


## What Research Questions Can Regression Answer

| Step | Question | Main tool |
|-----|----------|------|
| 1. Question | Prediction, description, comparison, or causal claim? | Context |

. . .

| Goal | MPG Example |
|-----|---------|
| Prediction | What highway MPG for a 3-liter engine? |
| Description | How does MPG vary with engine size? | 
| Comparison | How do automatic and manual transmissions differ in MPG? |
| Causal inference | Would changing $X$ change $Y$? |

. . .

::: danger
Causal inference requires a carefully designed study and additional assumptions.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note style="font-size: 1.2em"}

Description and comparison are **inferential** goals.

:::

 
::: notes

| Goal | Example question | Safe wording |
|-----|---------|--------|
| Prediction | What highway MPG for a 3-liter engine? | We predict... |
| Description | How does MPG vary with engine size? | MPG is associated with... |
| Comparison | How do auto and manual transmission differ in MPG? | The group difference is... |
| Causal inference | Would changing $X$ change $Y$? | With careful design of experiment and assumptions |

:::

## Fitting

| Step | Question | Main tool |
|-----|----------|------|

```{r}

ggplot(mpg_data, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 2.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "The regression line summarizes the conditional average",
    subtitle = "It does not claim that all cars with the same displacement have the same MPG",
    x = "Engine displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  )
```

<!-- Before finding the pattern that is most consistent with our data, we need a **model the fitting method applies to**. -->

To find the pattern most consistent with our data, we first need to specify the model being fitted.


# Simple Linear Regression Model

## Simple Linear Regression

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

For the $i$-th unit in the target population,

$$
\begin{align}
Y_i &= f(X_i) + \epsilon_i\\ &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i
\end{align}
$$

- $Y_i$: the response (random) variable
- $X_i$: **known fixed** value of the predictor
- $\epsilon_i$: random error with $\epsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)$
<!-- - $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are model coefficients. -->



| Piece | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i$ | systematic part |
| $\epsilon_i$ | deviation from the pattern |
| $\sigma$ | typical vertical scatter |

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: model-story-plot
#| out-width: 100%
set.seed(2)
story_dat <- tibble(x = seq(1, 6, length.out = 30)) |>
  mutate(mu = 38 - 3.2 * x,
         y = mu + rnorm(n(), 0, 3))
sel <- story_dat[c(8, 20, 26), ]
ggplot(story_dat, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mu), linewidth = 2) +
  geom_segment(data = sel, aes(xend = x, y = y, yend = mu), linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(data = sel, aes(y = mu), size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "True Regression Line and Errors",
    x = "X",
    y = "Y"
  )
```

<!-- - $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$ and $\sigma^2$ are **fixed unknown parameters** to be estimated from our collected data. -->

- $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, and $\sigma^2$ are **fixed but unknown parameters** to be estimated from the observed data.

:::

:::




::: notes
the *measurement error* model is
:::

## Regression Models a Conditional Distribution

<!-- When we collect data $\{ (x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots, (x_n, y_n)\},$ $y$ is assumed drawn from a normal distribution **conditional on the value of $x$**. Its value varies around its **conditional mean $\mu_{y \mid x}$**. -->

For data $\{(x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2),\dots,(x_n,y_n)\}$, each response $Y_i$ is assumed to be drawn from a normal distribution **conditional on $X_i=x_i$**. The response varies around its **conditional mean $\mu_{Y\mid X=x}$**.


```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
draw_panel(line_col = red_col, show_small = TRUE, show_bands = TRUE)
```

- The **mean response** of $Y$, $\mu_{Y\mid X}=E(Y\mid X)$, has a **straight-line** relationship with $X$, given by the population regression line $\mu_{Y\mid X}=\beta_0+\beta_1X$.

- The conditional variance of $Y$ does not depend on $X$.



::: notes
With the model, our first job is to collect data and estimate the unknown parameters $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$ and $\sigma^2$!
:::



## Model Assumptions

| Assumption | Model statement | What to check visually |
|-----|---------|------|
| Conditional mean | $E(Y\mid X=x)$ is approximately linear | Curved pattern? |
| Variability | Spread around the line is similar across $X$ | Fan shape? |
| Independence | Rows provide distinct information | Clustering in groups, time, or space? |
| Distribution | Residuals are approximately normal | Strong skewness or heavy tails? |


```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
draw_panel(line_col = red_col, show_small = TRUE, show_bands = TRUE)
```

::: notes

Do not present assumptions as a single all-or-nothing checklist. The mean model is usually the first priority for interpretation; dependence is often the first priority for uncertainty.

:::



# Parameter Estimation and Model Fitting

## Idea of Fitting

- Interested in $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ in the *sample* regression model:

\begin{align*}
y_i &= f(x_i) +  \epsilon_i \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1~x_{i} + \epsilon_i,
\end{align*}
or

$$E(y_i \mid x_i) = \mu_{y|x_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1~x_{i}$$

. . .

- Use sample statistics $b_0$ and $b_1$, computed from the data, to estimate $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$.

- $\hat{y}_{i}=b_0+b_1x_i$ is the **fitted value** at $x_i$. It estimates the conditional mean $\mu_{Y\mid X=x_i}$ and also serves as the point prediction for an individual response at $x_i$.

<!-- - $\hat{y}_{i} = b_0 + b_1~x_{i}$ predicted value -->





::: notes

- OK. once we collect the data, we have a sample regression model.
- Here I use small x and y to represent the collected data.
- Given this model, we're interested in $\beta_0$ (population parameter for the intercept) and $\beta_1$ (population parameter for the slope) because once we know $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$, we know the exact shape of $f$ and we know the relationship of $y$ and $x$, and given any value of $x$, we can predict its corresponding value of $y$ using the regression line $\hat{y}_{i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1~x_{i}$.
- But again the population parameters are unknown to us.
- $\hat{y}_i = E(Y|X_i=x_i)$
- $b_0$: intercept of the sample regression line
- $b_1$: slope of  the sample regression line

:::


## Fitting a Regression Line $\hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1X$

Given the data $\{ (x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots, (x_n, y_n)\},$

- Which *sample* regression line is the **best**? 
- Which estimates $b_0$ and $b_1$ provide the **best-fitting** line?


```{r}
#| out-width: 58%
load("./data/table11-1.rdata")
data <- `table11-1`
data <- data[order(data$x), ]
par(mar = c(3, 3, 1.5, 0), mgp = c(2, 0.5, 0))
plot(data$x, data$y, xlab = "x", ylab = "y", pch = 19, col = 4, las = 1, 
     ylim = c(0, 140), cex = 2, cex.main = 2,
     main = "Finding the best sample regression line")
abline(lm(data$y ~ data$x), col = "#003366", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(a = 30-6, b = 1.5, col = 1, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(a = 22-6, b = 1.7, col = 2, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(a = 15-6, b = 1.9, col = 3, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(a = 8-6, b = 2.1, col = 4, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(a = 1-6, b = 2.2, col = 5, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```


::: notes
- Now suppose we already get our sample, and now we are trying to use the sample to get a sample regression line, and hopefully, the sample regression line and the population regression line are alike. look similarly.
- So people usually ask
- Which *sample* regression line is the **best**? 
- What are the **best** estimators $b_0$ and $b_1$ for $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$?
- After all, given the data, we can generate so many different straight lines, and we need a criterion to help us determine which line is the best in some sense. Right!
:::



## MPG Data

```{r}
mpg_data <- mpg
reg_fit <- lm(hwy ~ displ, data = mpg_data)

p <- ggplot(data = reg_fit, 
            aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
     geom_point(alpha = 0.85) + 
     labs(title = "Highway MPG vs. Engine Displacement",
          x = "Displacement (litres)",
          y = "Highway miles per gallon")
p + theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "red", 
                                       face = "bold", 
                                       size = rel(1.5))) +
    labs(subtitle = "Just the data")
```

::: notes

That's see the idea of Ordinary Least Squares visually. Here just showed the data.
- Later we will work on the data set together.
<!-- - Do you see why some points are darker than some others? -->
<!-- - A darker point means that there are several identical (x, y) pairs, or replicates in the data set. -->

:::


## Fitted Line and Fitted Value

$\hat{y}_i = c_0 + c_1x_i$

```{r}
p + geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue", se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
    geom_point(mapping = aes(y = .fitted), color = "red", size = 2) +
    theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "red", 
                                       face = "bold", 
                                       size = rel(1.5))) +
    labs(subtitle = "Data + fitted line + fitted value")
```

::: notes

- All right, with the data, this figure also shows the least squares regression line, and the fitted value of $y$ for each $x$ in the training data, which are those red points.
- The fitted values of y are right on the regression line.
- Now the question is, how do we find this line?
- Given a line, we can have predicted values of y, right?
- Then what is residual on the plot? The residual will be the difference between the true observation y and the fitted value of y given any value of x.
- So a residual in the plot will be a vertical bar at the value of x with two ends of the bar $y$ and $\hat{y}$, right?
- (Show on board)
- (add $y_i = b_0+b_1x_i$ and residual line)

:::


## Residuals

- A **residual** is the difference between the observed response and the fitted response value, shown as a vertical bar.

- $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$

```{r}
p + geom_segment(mapping = aes(xend = displ, yend = .fitted),
                 color = "red", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue", se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "red", 
                                       face = "bold", 
                                       size = rel(1.5))) +
  labs(subtitle = "Data + fitted line + residuals")
```

::: notes

- Here shows all the residuals in vertical bars.
- least squares line is the line such that the sum of all the squared residuals is minimized.
- Why we square the residuals? 
- It's mathematically more convenient.
- Squaring emphasizes larger differences

:::


## What does "best" mean? Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)


Choose $b_0$ and $b_1$—and therefore the sample regression line—to minimize the **sum of squared residuals** $$SS_{res} = e_1^2 + e_2^2 + \dots + e_n^2 = \sum_{i = 1}^n e_i^2.$$


<!-- Choose the *best* $b_0$ and $b_1$ or the sample regression line minimizing the **sum of squared residuals** $$SS_{res} = e_1^2 + e_2^2 + \dots + e_n^2 = \sum_{i = 1}^n e_i^2.$$ -->

. . .

- Substituting $e_i=y_i-(b_0+b_1x_i)$ into $SS_{res}$ gives

$$\begin{align} SS_{res}(b_0, b_1) &= (y_1 - b_0 - b_1x_1)^2 + (y_2 - b_0 - b_1x_2)^2 + \dots + (y_n - b_0 - b_1x_n)^2\\ &= \sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - b_0 - b_1x_i)^2 \end{align}$$ 


- The resulting value is no larger than $\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-a_0-a_1x_i)^2$ for any other pair $(a_0,a_1)\ne(b_0,b_1)$.

<!-- that is the smallest comparing to any other $\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - a_0 - a_1x_i)^2$ that uses another pair of estimators $(a_0, a_1) \ne (b_0, b_1)$. -->



::: notes

- Now the question is How do we get $b_0$ and $b_1$ that well estimate $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$? 
- We choose $b_0$ and $b_1$, or regression line $b_0 + b_1x$ that minimizes the **sum of squared residuals**.
- If we define residual as $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$, then the sum of squared residuals is $\sum_{i = 1}^n e_i^2$.
- And this approach that estimates the population parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ or the population regression line is called Ordinary Least Squares method.

:::


## 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(broom)
library(patchwork)

ols_intercept <- coef(reg_fit)[["(Intercept)"]]
ols_slope <- coef(reg_fit)[["displ"]]

# augment.lm creates .fitted and .resid
reg_fit_aug <- augment(reg_fit, data = mpg_data) %>%
  mutate(
    ols_fitted = .fitted,
    ols_resid = .resid
  )

# OLS residual sum of squares
ols_rss <- sum(reg_fit_aug$ols_resid^2)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct a deliberately non-optimal line
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Use only 60% of the OLS slope
bad_slope <- 0.10 * ols_slope

# Make the line pass through (mean x, mean y)
bad_intercept <- mean(mpg_data$hwy) -
  bad_slope * mean(mpg_data$displ)

reg_fit_aug <- reg_fit_aug %>%
  mutate(
    bad_fitted = bad_intercept + bad_slope * displ,
    bad_resid = hwy - bad_fitted
  )

# RSS for the non-optimal line
bad_rss <- sum(reg_fit_aug$bad_resid^2)

# Numerical comparison
rss_comparison <- tibble(
  line = c("OLS line", "Non-optimal line"),
  intercept = c(ols_intercept, bad_intercept),
  slope = c(ols_slope, bad_slope),
  RSS = c(ols_rss, bad_rss)
)
```

## Least Squares Estimates

- The least-squares approach chooses $b_0$ and $b_1$ to minimize $SS_{res}$:
$$(b_0, b_1) = \arg\min_{\alpha_0, \alpha_1} \sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \alpha_0 - \alpha_1x_i)^2$$
. . .

$$ \color{red}{b_0 = \overline{y} - b_1\overline{x}}$$


$$\color{red}{b_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \overline{x})^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = r \frac{\sqrt{S_{yy}}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}},$$ where $S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \overline{x})^2$, $S_{yy} = \sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \overline{y})^2$, $S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y})$, and $r$ is the sample correlation coefficient between $x$ and $y$.

. . .

::: question
What can we learn from the formulas for $b_0$ and $b_1$?
:::


::: notes
- The LS regression line passes through the centroid.
- $b_1$ is kinda like a scaled covariance of X and Y.
- $b_0$ and $b_1$ are correlated.
:::


## Why squared residuals matter {visibility="hidden"}

| Residual | Absolute error | Squared error | Consequence |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | small penalty |
| 2 | 2 | 4 | larger penalty |
| 5 | 5 | 25 | very large penalty |
| 10 | 10 | 100 | can dominate the fit |


::: {.fragment}

**Least squares is sensitive to large residuals.** That is useful when large errors really matter, dangerous when they are mistakes or special cases.

:::

## Formula, but only the useful version {visibility="hidden"}

$$
(b_0,b_1)=\arg\min_{a,b}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-a-bx_i)^2
$$

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

| Quantity | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| $b_1$ | estimated change in mean $Y$ per 1-unit increase in $X$ |
| $b_0$ | estimated mean $Y$ when $X=0$ |
| $\hat y_i$ | fitted mean at $x_i$ |
| $e_i$ | remaining error after using the line |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Key point:** fitting is not the hard part. The hard part is deciding whether the fitted line answers the question.

:::
:::

## Indicator Variables

Define a binary indicator variable:

$$
x_i =
\begin{cases}
0, & \text{automatic},\\
1, & \text{manual}.
\end{cases}
$$

The regression model is

$$
hwy_i = \beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i.
$$

| Coefficient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\beta_0$ | Mean highway MPG for automatic transmission |
| $\beta_1$ | Manual mean minus automatic mean |
| $\beta_0+\beta_1$ | Mean highway MPG for manual transmission |


. . .

The fitted regression model is

$$
\widehat{hwy}_i = b_0+b_1 x_i
$$



::: notes

- A regression predictor does not have to be quantitative.
- Transmission type has two categories: automatic and manual.
- We represent transmission type using an indicator variable.
- Automatic transmission is the reference category and is assigned a value of zero.
- Manual transmission is assigned a value of one.
- The regression coefficient beta one is therefore a difference between two group means.
- This illustrates an important general idea: a comparison between two groups can be written as a regression model.

:::


## The Slope is a Mean Difference


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
trans_fit <- lm(hwy ~ trans, data = mpg_new)
coef(trans_fit)
```

::: center

$\widehat{hwy}_i = 22.29+3.49 x_i$

:::
  
<!-- The fitted regression model is -->

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \widehat{hwy}_i -->
<!-- = -->
<!-- `r sprintf("%.2f", b0)` -->
<!-- + -->
<!-- `r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`M_i. -->
<!-- $$ -->

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Auto $x_i=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{hwy}_{\text{auto}}
&=
`r sprintf("%.2f", b0)`
+
`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`(0)\\
&=
`r sprintf("%.2f", b0)`
\text{ MPG}
\end{aligned}
$$

**$b_0$ is the mean highway MPG for the [reference (baseline)]{.red} category.**

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Manual $x_i=1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{hwy}_{\text{manual}}
&=
`r sprintf("%.2f", b0)`
+
`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`(1)\\
&=
`r sprintf("%.2f", b0 + b1)`
\text{ MPG}
\end{aligned}
$$

**$b_0+b_1$ is the mean highway MPG for [manual]{.red} transmission.**

:::

::::

::: {.fragment}

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \underbrace{ -->
<!-- `r sprintf("%.2f", b0 + b1)` -->
<!-- }_{\text{manual mean}} -->
<!-- - -->
<!-- \underbrace{ -->
<!-- `r sprintf("%.2f", b0)` -->
<!-- }_{\text{automatic mean}} -->
<!-- = -->
<!-- \underbrace{ -->
<!-- `r sprintf("%.2f", b1)` -->
<!-- }_{\text{regression coefficient}} -->
<!-- $$ -->

- **Slope:** Cars with manual transmissions are expected to have 3.49 MPG higher highway fuel economy, on average, than cars with automatic transmissions.
  + The coefficient compares the other level (`trans = manual`) with the baseline (`trans = auto`).


:::

::: notes

- When the indicator variable equals zero, the fitted value equals the intercept.
- Therefore, the intercept is the mean highway MPG for automatic-transmission configurations.
- When the indicator variable equals one, the fitted value is the intercept plus the manual-transmission coefficient.
- The slope is exactly the difference between the two group means.
- We should interpret this as an observed comparison or association, not as a causal effect.
- The data do not establish that changing a vehicle from automatic to manual transmission would cause highway MPG to increase by this amount.
- Automatic and manual vehicle configurations can also differ in engine displacement, vehicle class, manufacturer, and other characteristics.

:::

```{r}
#| label: prepare-transmission-reg-example

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

mpg_new <- ggplot2::mpg |>

ybar0 <- trans_summary |>

ybar1 <- trans_summary |>

eq_lab <- paste0(

  ifelse(b1 >= 0, " + ", " - "),
```

## Estimation for $\sigma^2$

- Think of $\sigma^2$ as the **variance around the population regression line**.

- The estimate of $\sigma^2$, denoted by $s^2$ or $\hat{\sigma}^2$, is computed from the data as
$$s^2 = \frac{SS_{res}}{df_{res}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n-2} = MS_{res}$$

<!-- - Think of $\sigma^2$ as **variance around the line** or the **mean squared error**. -->

<!-- - The estimate of $\sigma^2$, denoted as $s^2$ or $\hat{\sigma}^$, computed from the data is  -->
<!-- $$s^2 = \frac{SS_{res}}{df_{res}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n-2} = MS_{res}$$ -->

<!-- - $s$: the **residual standard error** or **standard error of regression**, is a measure of the *lack of fit* of the regression model to the data. -->

- $s$, the **residual standard error**, estimates the typical vertical distance between an observed response and the fitted line.


. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output.lines: !expr c(15, 16)
#| code-line-numbers: false
(summ_reg_fit <- summary(reg_fit))
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
summ_reg_fit$sigma
```


::: notes

- So we are done estimation for $beta$. Let's talk about the estimation of $\sigma^2$.
- The estimate of $\sigma^2$, denoted as $s^2$ or $s_{\epsilon}^2$, based on the sample data is residual sum of squares divided by $n-2$, the degrees of freedom
- It can be shown that $E(SS_{res}) = (n-2)\sigma^2$. That is, $s^2$ is an *unbiased* estimator for $\sigma^2$. `r emo::ji('thumbsup')`
- measure of the *lack of fit* of the regression model to the data.

:::



## Measure of the *Lack of Fit*

- If $\hat{y}_i \approx y_i$, then $s$ will be small, and the model fits the data well.

<!-- - If $\hat{y}_i$ is far away from $y_i$, $s$ may be large, indicating the model does not fit the data well.  -->

- If many fitted values $\hat y_i$ are far from the observed responses $y_i$, then $s$ will be large, indicating substantial unexplained variation or model misspecification.


```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.3
#| out-width: 100%
par(mar = c(3, 3, 1.5, 1), mgp = c(2, 1, 0))
x <- seq(-1, 2, length  = 50)
y_small <- 2 + 1 * x + rnorm(50, 0, .5)
y_mis <- 2 + 1 * x^2 + rnorm(50, 0, .5)
y_vio <- 2 + 1 * x + rnorm(50, 0, sqrt(seq(0, 3, length = 50)))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(x, y_small, main = "small var", ylab = "y", las = 1,
     col = 4, pch = 16, ylim = c(0, 8), cex.main = 1.9)
abline(lm(y_small~x), col = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(a = 2, b = 1, col = 1, lwd = 1)
legend("topleft", c("fitted", "true"), col = c(2, 1), lwd = c(2, 1), bty = "n")
plot(x, y_mis, main = "large var: model misspecified", ylab = "y", las = 1,
     col = 4, pch = 16, ylim = c(0, 8), cex.main = 1.9)
abline(lm(y_mis~x), col = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(x, 2 + 1 * x^2, col = 1, lwd = 1)
plot(x, y_vio, main = "large var: assumption violated", ylab = "y", las = 1,
     col = 4, pch = 16, ylim = c(0, 8), cex.main = 1.9)
abline(lm(y_vio~x), col = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(a = 2, b = 1, col = 1, lwd = 1)
```



::: notes

- If the fitted value using the model is close to the true value, $\hat{y}_i \approx y_i$, then $s$ will be small, and the model fits the data well. 
- If $\hat{y}_i$ is far away from $y_i$, $s$ may be large, indicating that the model does not fit the data well. 
- Let's see the example shown below. If X and Y have a linear relationship and the relationship is pretty tight, we should see the fitted values on the fitted line are close to the observations, and the $s$ will be small.
- But if X and Y have a quadratic relationship, but we fit a linear regression, the fitted values will be distant from the observations, and $s$ may be large.
- The case on the right shows the violation of constant variance. In this case, the fitted values are away from the observations too, resulting in large $s$, and indicating the model does not fit the data well. OK.

:::




# Uncertainty Quantification 



## Sampling Variation

- Our data are **one realization** among many possible data sets generated by a true data-generating process described by a regression model.

- **[Repeated Sampling]** If we collected another data set, we would obtain a different pair $(b_0, b_1)$.

- Suppose the true model is $Y_i = 5 + 2X_i + \epsilon_i$, $\epsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, 25)$

. . .

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 1. Specify the true data-generating process
#--------------------------------------------------

set.seed(4780)

n <- 30

beta_0 <- 5
beta_1 <- 2
sigma  <- 5

# Use the same predictor values in both samples
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = n)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 2. Generate two independent samples
#    from the same regression model
#--------------------------------------------------

sample_1 <- tibble(
    sample = "Sample 1",
    x = x,
    epsilon = rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma),
    y = beta_0 + beta_1 * x + epsilon
)

sample_2 <- tibble(
    sample = "Sample 2",
    x = x,
    epsilon = rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma),
    y = beta_0 + beta_1 * x + epsilon
)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 3. Fit separate regression models
#--------------------------------------------------

fit_1 <- lm(y ~ x, data = sample_1)
fit_2 <- lm(y ~ x, data = sample_2)

b_0_1 <- coef(fit_1)[1]
b_1_1 <- coef(fit_1)[2]

b_0_2 <- coef(fit_2)[1]
b_1_2 <- coef(fit_2)[2]

# Fitted-line equations shown in the plots
equation_1 <- sprintf(
    "Fitted line:  y-hat = %.2f %+.2f x",
    b_0_1, b_1_1
)

equation_2 <- sprintf(
    "Fitted line:  y-hat = %.2f %+.2f x",
    b_0_2, b_1_2
)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 4. Use common axis limits for fair comparison
#--------------------------------------------------

combined_data <- bind_rows(sample_1, sample_2)

y_limits <- range(
    combined_data$y,
    beta_0 + beta_1 * x
)

y_padding <- 0.08 * diff(y_limits)

common_y_limits <- c(
    y_limits[1] - y_padding,
    y_limits[2] + y_padding
)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 5. Create a plotting function
#--------------------------------------------------

make_sampling_plot <- function(data, fit, equation, title) {
    
    ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
        
        # Observed data
        geom_point(
            size = 3,
            alpha = 0.75
        ) +
        
        # True population regression line
        geom_abline(
            intercept = beta_0,
            slope = beta_1,
            linewidth = 2
        ) +
        
        # Estimated regression line
        geom_abline(
            intercept = coef(fit)[1],
            slope = coef(fit)[2],
            linewidth = 2,
            linetype = "dashed",
            colour = "blue"
        ) +
        
        # Estimated equation
        annotate(
            "label",
            x = -Inf,
            y = Inf,
            label = equation,
            hjust = -0.05,
            vjust = 1.3,
            size = 10,
            label.size = 0.25
        ) +
        
        scale_x_continuous(
            limits = range(x),
            expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.03))
        ) +
        
        scale_y_continuous(
            limits = common_y_limits,
            expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
        ) +
        
        labs(
            title = title,
            # subtitle = paste0(
            #     "Same true model:  Y = ",
            #     beta_0, " + ", beta_1,
            #     "x + epsilon,   epsilon ~ N(0, ",
            #     sigma^2, ")"
            # ),
            x = expression(x),
            y = expression(y),
            # caption = "Dashed line: true regression line    Solid line: fitted regression line"
        ) +
        
        theme_classic(base_size = 18) +
        
        theme(
            plot.title = element_text(
                face = "bold",
                size = 17
            ),
            plot.subtitle = element_text(
                size = 11
            ),
            plot.caption = element_text(
                hjust = 0,
                size = 10
            ),
            axis.title = element_text(
                face = "bold"
            )
        )
}

#--------------------------------------------------
# 6. Produce the two plots
#--------------------------------------------------

p1 <- make_sampling_plot(
    data = sample_1,
    fit = fit_1,
    equation = equation_1,
    title = ""
)

p2 <- make_sampling_plot(
    data = sample_2,
    fit = fit_2,
    equation = equation_2,
    title = ""
)
```

## Sampling Variation

- We quantify the sampling variation of $(b_0,b_1)$ to assess the uncertainty in using them to estimate $(\beta_0,\beta_1)$.

- If $\epsilon_i\stackrel{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)$, we can derive the exact sampling distributions of $b_0$ and $b_1$.[^1]

[^1]: We can also derive an exact sampling distribution for an estimator of $\sigma^2$. The framework used in this course for inference, prediction, and uncertainty quantification is the **frequentist** approach.

. . . 

These sampling distributions yield confidence intervals (CIs) for $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$:

- A $(1-\alpha)100\%$ CI for $\beta_1$ is $\small \boxed{b_1\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}\,se(b_1)}$, where $se(b_1)$ is the standard error of $b_1$.

- A 95% CI for $\beta_1$ is approximately $\small \boxed{b_1\pm2\,se(b_1)}$.

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
confint(reg_fit)
```

. . .

::: danger

We would never know whether the CI covers the true parameter values or not.

:::


::: notes

summ_reg_fit$coefficients

:::

<!-- # Learning from Simulation -->



<!-- ## Fake-data simulation workflow -->

<!-- | Step | What we do | Why | -->
<!-- |---|---|---| -->
<!-- | 1 | Choose a known data-generating model | truth is known | -->
<!-- | 2 | Simulate many datasets | see sample-to-sample variation | -->
<!-- | 3 | Fit the same regression each time | test the workflow | -->
<!-- | 4 | Compare estimates to truth | learn what uncertainty means | -->




## Generating Sampling Distribution from Simulation


::: {.instructions}

**Algorithm**  

- [Create the pretend world]{.blue}
  + A true regression model
  
- [Repeat sampling $M$ times]{.blue}
  + Generate $M$ data sets of size $n$ from the true model: $D^1, \dots, D^M$

- [Fit the model $M$ times]{.blue}
  + For each data set $D^m, m = 1, \dots, M$, compute the estimate $b_1^m$ and confidence intervals $CI^m$

- [Quantify uncertainty]{.blue}
  + Plot a histogram of the $M$ estimates $b_1^1, \dots, b_1^M$ to visualize sampling variation
  + Compute the percentage of confidence intervals that contain the true value

:::



<!-- ::: algo -->


<!-- - Create the pretend world  -->
<!--  + Set the true regression model -->

<!-- - Simulate  -->


<!-- ::: -->



<!-- ## Same Truth, Different Data -->

##

- True model: $Y_i = 5 + 2X_i + \epsilon_i$, $\epsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, 25)$

- Generate $M=100$ simulated data sets, each of size $n=50$.

- Each data set produces a different pair $(b_0,b_1)$.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2026)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 1. Simulation settings
#--------------------------------------------------

true_b0 <- 5
true_b1 <- 2
sigma   <- 5

n_sim     <- 100
n          <- 50
conf_level <- 0.95

x_grid <- seq(1, 6, length.out = 60)


#--------------------------------------------------
# 2. Create one organized simulation data frame
#--------------------------------------------------

sim_df <- tibble(
  sample = seq_len(n_sim)
) |>
  mutate(

    # Generate one dataset for each simulation
    data = map(sample, \(s) {

      x <- runif(n, min = 1, max = 6)

      y <- true_b0 +
        true_b1 * x +
        rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma)

      tibble(x = x, y = y)
    }),

    # Fit a regression model to each dataset
    fit = map(
      data,
      \(dat) lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
    ),

    # Extract estimated coefficients
    intercept = map_dbl(
      fit,
      \(model) coef(model)[["(Intercept)"]]
    ),

    slope = map_dbl(
      fit,
      \(model) coef(model)[["x"]]
    ),

    # Extract standard error of the estimated slope
    slope_se = map_dbl(
      fit,
      \(model) coef(summary(model))["x", "Std. Error"]
    ),

    # Residual degrees of freedom
    residual_df = map_int(
      fit,
      df.residual
    ),

    # Critical t value
    t_star = qt(
      1 - (1 - conf_level) / 2,
      df = residual_df
    ),

    # Confidence interval for beta_1
    lower = slope - t_star * slope_se,
    upper = slope + t_star * slope_se,

    # Does the interval contain the true slope?
    covered = lower <= true_b1 & true_b1 <= upper,

    # Coordinates for plotting each fitted line
    fitted_line = map(
      fit,
      \(model) {
        tibble(
          x = x_grid,
          yhat = predict(
            model,
            newdata = tibble(x = x_grid)
          )
        )
      }
    )
  )
```


```{r}
#| label: fake-lines
#| out-width: 100%

truth_dat <- tibble(
  x = x_grid,
  y = true_b0 + true_b1 * x_grid
)

line_plot_df <- sim_df |>
  filter(sample <= 100) |>
  select(sample, fitted_line) |>
  unnest(fitted_line)

p_lines <- ggplot(
  line_plot_df,
  aes(
    x = x,
    y = yhat,
    group = sample
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    alpha = 0.10,
    colour = 4
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = truth_dat,
    aes(x = x, y = y),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.5,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Same Truth, Different Data, Different Fitted Lines",
    x = "X",
    y = "Y"
  )

p_lines
```

## Coverage Probabilities

- $\text{Empirical coverage}=\dfrac{\text{number of CIs containing }\beta_1}{M}$


```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
coverage_probability <- mean(sim_df$covered)
number_missed <- sum(!sim_df$covered)

p_confidence_intervals <- ggplot(
  sim_df,
  aes(
    x = sample,
    y = slope,
    colour = covered
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = true_b1,
    colour = "red",
    linewidth = 2
  ) +
  geom_linerange(
    aes(
      ymin = lower,
      ymax = upper
    ),
    linewidth = 1.2,
    alpha = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 1.2,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE"  = 4,
      "FALSE" = "#E69F00"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "TRUE"  = "Contains true slope",
      "FALSE" = "Misses true slope"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = NULL,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.005, 0.005))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = expression(
      "95% Confidence Intervals for " * beta[1]
    ),
    # subtitle = sprintf(
    #   "%d intervals missed the true slope; empirical coverage = %.1f%%",
    #   number_missed,
    #   100 * coverage_probability
    # ),
    x = "Simulated sample",
    y = expression(
      "95% confidence interval"
    )
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

p_confidence_intervals
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
coverage_summary <- sim_df |>
  summarise(
    number_of_simulations = n(),
    number_covered = sum(covered),
    number_missed = sum(!covered),
    coverage_probability = mean(covered),
    coverage_percent = 100 * mean(covered),
    monte_carlo_se = sqrt(
      coverage_probability *
        (1 - coverage_probability) /
        number_of_simulations
    )
  )

coverage_summary
```



## What uncertainty is trying to say {visibility="hidden"}

::: danger


| Output | Better interpretation | Common misuse |
|---|---|---|
| Estimate | best single-number summary from this data/model | the truth |
| Standard error | typical estimation noise | measurement error of $Y$ |
| Confidence interval | plausible values under the model | probability the fixed parameter is in this one interval |
| p-value | incompatibility with a point null | probability the null is true |


:::


<!-- # Inference without overemphasizing tests -->

## Testing the slope: what the test can and cannot say {visibility="hidden"}

| Result | What it supports | What it does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| small p-value | data are not very compatible with zero slope under the model | the relationship is linear |
| large p-value | slope is not precisely distinguished from zero | no relationship exists |
| narrow interval | slope is estimated precisely | model assumptions are correct |
| wide interval | data are not very informative | the effect is unimportant |



## Hypothesis Testing

- <span style="color:blue"> $H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_1^0 \quad H_1: \beta_1 \ne \beta_1^0$  </span>

- Under $H_0$, the test statistic is $t_{test}=\dfrac{b_1-\color{red}{\beta_1^0}}{se(b_1)}\sim t_{n-2}$.

- Reject $H_0$ in favor of $H_1$ if 
  + $|t_{test}| > t_{\alpha/2, \, n-2}$ (critical value method)
  + $\text{p-value} = 2P(t_{n-2} > |t_{test}|) < \alpha$ (p-value method)
 
. . .


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
summ_reg_fit$coefficients
```

- By default, `summary()` tests $H_0:\beta_0=0$ and $H_0:\beta_1=0$.

::: notes
- in addition to estimation, we may be interested in testing.
- To do the testing on $\beta_1$, the testing procedure is basically the same as the procedure for population mean $\mu$ we reviewed last week.
- Usually $\beta_1^0 = 0$, but we may be interested in other values.
- good growth $\beta_1 > 2$
car::linearHypothesis()
:::



## Interpretation of Testing Results

- <span style="color:blue"> $H_0: \beta_1 = 0 \quad H_1: \beta_1 \ne 0$ </span>
- *Failing to reject $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$* (large p-value) means that the slope is not estimated precisely enough to distinguish it from zero.
  + It does not mean the slope is exactly zero
  + It does not *prove* that no linear relationship exists
  + A nonlinear relationship may still exist.


::: notes

- So back to the testing on $\beta_1$.
- If we do not reject $H_0$, it implies there is **no linear relationship** between $Y$ and $X$. Right? Because $\beta_1$, the slope of the regression line is pretty much 0. 
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.5
#| out-width: 50%
set.seed(9274)
x1 <- seq(0, 6, by = 0.05)
y_u <- (x1-3)^2 - 4 + rnorm(length(x1), mean = 0, sd = 1)
x2 <- seq(-8, -2, by = 0.05)
y_none <- rnorm(length(x2), mean = 0, sd = 1)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(y_none ~ x2, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", pch = 19, col = "lightblue")
abline(h = 0, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
plot(y_u ~ x1, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", pch = 19, col = "lightblue")
abline(h = 0, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
```


::: notes
- But it actually has two cases. One $x$ and $y$ may have no relationship at all, or they don't have linear relationship but have another kind of relationship, like quadratic.
- So we have to be careful when we interpret the testing result. OK.
:::

::: notes
We have to be more careful and precise on what we are claiming.
:::



## Interpretation of Testing Results

- *Rejecting $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$* (small p-value) means that the data are not very compatible with a zero slope under the model.

- The result is consistent with several possibilities:
  + the straight-line model may be adequate
  + it does not prove that the relationship is linear
  + another model may describe the relationship better
  
```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.5
#| out-width: 45%
set.seed(9274)
x <- seq(-3, 4, 0.05)
y_s <-  -0.5 * x^3 + x^2 + x + rnorm(length(x), mean = 0, sd = 2)
y_pos_lin_strong <- 3 * x + rnorm(length(x), mean = 0, sd = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(y_pos_lin_strong ~ x, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", pch = 19, col = "lightblue")
abline(lm(y_pos_lin_strong ~ x), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
plot(y_s ~ x, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", pch = 19, col = "lightblue")
abline(lm(y_s ~ x), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
```


::: notes

- *Rejecting $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$* (small p-value) means data are not very compatible with zero slope under the model.

- It could mean 
  + the straight-line model is adequate
  + it does not prove the relationship is linear
  + better results could be obtained with a more complicated model even though there is a linear effect of $x$ , even though the fitted linear slope differs from zero.
  
  
:::



# Prediction

## Fitting and Predicting

- **Fitting** uses the observed data to estimate a model.

- **Prediction** applies the fitted model to unseen data.
  + We use the model to predict a response at a new predictor value $x^{new}$.

. . .

- Two prediction targets:

  + **Mean response:** <span style="color:blue">The **mean** highway MPG, $E(Y\mid X=x^{new})$, for cars with $x^{new}=3$ liters of displacement.</span>
  
  + **New observation:** <span style="color:blue">The highway MPG, $Y^{new}$, of **one future car** with $x^{new}=3$ liters of displacement.</span>
  
::: question
Which prediction is harder? 🤔
:::
  
## Point Prediction

- The fitted value on the regression line is the point prediction for both the mean response and a new observation.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
predict(reg_fit, newdata = data.frame(displ = 3))
```

```{r}
p + geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue", se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 1.1) +
    annotate("point", x = 3, y = 35.698-3.531*3, color = "red", size = 5) +
    annotate("label", x = 3, y = 43, label = "new car:\n3.0 L", size = 5)
```


::: notes
| Target | Question | Usually shown as |
|---|---|---|
| Fitted value | What does the fitted line say at $x_0$? | point on line |
| Mean response | What is the average $Y$ among units with $X=x_0$? | confidence interval/band |
| New observation | What might one future $Y$ be at $X=x_0$? | prediction interval/band |
:::


## Predictive Uncertainty

<!-- - **Mean response**: The *linear predictor* $\beta_0 + \beta_1x^{new}$ propagates the inferential uncertainty in $(\beta_0, \beta_1)$. -->
<!--   + represents the distribution of uncertainty about the expected or average value of $y$ for new data points with predictors $x^{new}$ -->

<!-- - **New observation**: The predictive distribution for a new observation, $\beta_0 + \beta_1x^{new} + \epsilon$: -->
<!--   + represents uncertainty about a new observation $y^{new}$ with predictors $x^{new}$ -->


- **Mean response:** Uncertainty arises because $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are estimated from a sample.
  + It quantifies uncertainty about the expected response $E(Y\mid X=x^{new}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x^{new}$.
  
- **New observation:** The predictive distribution includes both parameter-estimation uncertainty and a new random error $\epsilon$, $\beta_0 + \beta_1x^{new} + \epsilon$.
  + It quantifies uncertainty about one future response $Y^{new}$ at $x^{new}$.



. . .

::: question
Which uncertainty is larger? 🤔
:::
  
. . .

::: danger

- As sample size approaches infinity, $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are estimated more and more precisely, and the uncertainty in the linear predictor approaches zero.

- Uncertainty for a new observation does not approach zero; it approaches irreducible error standard deviation $\sigma$.

:::


## Interval Prediction

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

With $\epsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)$, we have

- The $(1-\alpha)100\%$ CI for $E(y\mid x^{new})$ is $$\small (b_0+b_1x^{new}) \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-2} S\sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^{new} - \overline{x})^2}{S_{xx}}}$$

- The $(1-\alpha)100\%$ **prediction interval** (PI) for $y(x^{new})$ is $$\small (b_0+b_1x^{new}) \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-2} S\sqrt{ {\color{red}{1}} + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^{new} - \overline{x})^2}{S_{xx}}}$$

::: fragment

- *The PI is wider because it includes uncertainty about $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ as well as the random error $\epsilon$*.

:::

:::


::: {.column width="50%"}

::: fragment

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
## CI for the mean response
predict(reg_fit, 
        newdata = data.frame(displ = 3), 
        interval = "confidence", 
        level = 0.95)
```


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
## PI for a new observation
predict(reg_fit, 
        newdata = data.frame(displ = 3), 
        interval = "prediction", 
        level = 0.95)
```

:::

:::

::::




## Confidence Interval vs. Prediction Interval

```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
par(mar = c(3, 3, 0, 0), mgp = c(2, 0.5, 0))
## Data and regression line
plot(x = mpg$displ, y = mpg$hwy, las = 1, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, ylim = c(7.5, 45),
     xlab = "Displacement (litres)", ylab = "Highway MPG")
legend("topright", c("CI for the mean response", "PI for a new observation"), 
       col = c("red", "green3"), lwd = c(3, 3), bty = "n")
abline(reg_fit, col = "blue", lwd = 3) # abline(a = 47.475, b = -7.859, col = "#003366", lwd = 3)
segments(x0 = 3.02, y0 = 24.6, y1 = 25.6, col = "red", lwd = 4)
segments(x0 = 2.98, y0 = 17.5, y1 = 32.7, col = "green3", lwd = 4)
abline(h = 25.1, lty = 2)
```



## Confidence Interval vs. Prediction Interval

The interval is shortest when $x^{new} = \bar{x}$!

```{r}
par(mar = c(3, 3, 0, 0), mgp = c(2, 0.5, 0))
plot(x = mpg$displ, y = mpg$hwy, las = 1, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, ylim = c(4, 45),
     xlab = "Displacement (litres)", ylab = "Highway MPG")
newx <- seq(min(mpg$displ), max(mpg$displ), by = 0.1)
ci <- predict(reg_fit, newdata = data.frame(displ = newx), interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)
pi <- predict(reg_fit, newdata = data.frame(displ = newx), interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)
lines(newx, ci[, 1], col = "blue", lwd = 2)
matlines(newx, ci[, 2:3], col = "red", lty = 1, lwd = 2)
matlines(newx, pi[, 2:3], col = "green3", lty = 1, lwd = 2)
abline(v = mean(mpg$displ))
segments(x0 = 3.02, y0 = 24.6, y1 = 25.6, col = "red", lwd = 4)
segments(x0 = 2.98, y0 = 17.5, y1 = 32.7, col = "green3", lwd = 4)
legend("topright", c("Fitted line", "CI", "PI"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 1), lwd = c(3, 3, 3), col = c("blue", "red", "green3"), bty = "n")
```


## Interpolation vs extrapolation {visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: extrapolation-plot
x_ext <- seq(0.5, 8.5, length.out = 160)
line_ext <- as.data.frame(predict(fit_mpg, newdata = data.frame(displ = x_ext), interval = "prediction"))
ext_df <- tibble(displ = x_ext, fit = line_ext$fit, lwr = line_ext$lwr, upr = line_ext$upr)
obs_range <- range(mpg_data$displ)

ggplot(mpg_data, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_rect(data = tibble(xmin = obs_range[1], xmax = obs_range[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_ribbon(data = ext_df, aes(x = displ, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(data = ext_df, aes(y = fit), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(obs_range), y = 45, label = "data-supported range", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = 45, label = "extrapolation", size = 5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 8.5), ylim = c(5, 48)) +
  labs(x = "Engine displacement (liters)", y = "Highway MPG")
```



## {background-iframe="https://chenghanyustats-introstat-regression-ci.share.connect.posit.cloud/" background-interactive="true"}


## Prediction requires available predictors {visibility="hidden"}

| Predictor type | Safe for future prediction? | Example |
|---|---|---|
| measured before prediction time | usually yes | engine displacement |
| measured after the outcome | no | final exam score to predict course grade |
| derived using the outcome | no | rank computed after observing $Y$ |
| forecasted predictor | maybe | economic growth forecast for election prediction |



# Model Checking

## A Fitted Line Can Miss Curvature

```{r}
#| label: nonlinear-miss
set.seed(479)
curve_dat <- tibble(x = runif(120, 0, 10)) |>
  mutate(y = 18 + 3.8 * x - 0.35 * x^2 + rnorm(n(), 0, 2.5))
fit_curve_line <- lm(y ~ x, data = curve_dat)
curve_aug <- curve_dat |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(fit_curve_line), resid = resid(fit_curve_line))

ggplot(curve_dat, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 2.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "A line can be fit even when the pattern is not linear",
    # subtitle = "Solid: linear fit. Dashed: flexible smooth.",
    x = "X",
    y = "Y"
  )
```


## Residuals: what remains after the line?  {visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: residual-plot-mpg
mpg_aug <- mpg_data |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(fit_mpg), resid = resid(fit_mpg))

ggplot(mpg_aug, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 2.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Residual plot: look for remaining structure",
    x = "Fitted highway MPG",
    y = "Residual"
  )
```


## Graphical Diagnostics: Residual Plot

- Residuals should be distributed randomly around 0.
- Check this by plotting residuals against the fitted value of $y$: $e_i$ vs. $\hat{y}_i$
- Look for a roughly horizontal band with no systematic pattern.


```{r}
#| purl: false
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 56%
df <- tibble(
    fake_resid = rnorm(1000, mean = 0, sd = 30),
    fake_predicted = runif(1000, min = 0, max = 200)
)
ggplot(df, mapping = aes(x = fake_predicted, y = fake_resid)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
    labs(x = "Predicted (y_hat)", y = "Residuals (e)")
```

::: notes
We are looking for
- Residuals distributed randomly around 0.
- With no visible pattern along the $x$ or $y$ axes.
- This can be checked by plotting residuals against the fitted value of $y$.
- Here shows a good residual plot. Residuals are around 0, and its variation is more or less the same across different values of $\hat{y}$.
- There is no significant pattern in the plot.
:::

## Residual Pattern Reveals the Miss

```{r}
#| label: nonlinear-resid

ggplot(curve_aug, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 2.1) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Curvature shows up as structure in residuals",
    x = "Fitted value",
    y = "Residual"
  )
```

## Not looking for...

:::{.large}
**Fan shapes**
:::

```{r}
#| purl: false
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 60%
set.seed(12346)
df <- tibble(
  fake_resid = c(rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 1), 
                 rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 15), 
                 rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 25), 
                 rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 20), 
                 rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 25), 
                 rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 50), 
                 rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 35), 
                 rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 40),
                 rnorm(200, mean = 0, sd = 80)),
  fake_predicted = seq(0.2, 200, 0.2)
)
ggplot(df, mapping = aes(x = fake_predicted, y = fake_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted (y_hat)", y = "Residuals (e)")
```

::: notes
- We are not looking for a plot that has a fan shape.
:::



## Not looking for...

:::{.large}
**Distinct groups or clusters**
:::

```{r}
#| purl: false
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 60%
set.seed(12346)
df <- tibble(
  fake_predicted = seq(0.2, 200, 0.2),
  fake_resid = c(
    rnorm(500, mean = -20, sd = 10),
    rnorm(500, mean = 10, sd = 10)
  )
)
ggplot(df, mapping = aes(x = fake_predicted, y = fake_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted (y_hat)", y = "Residuals (e)")
```


::: notes
- We are not looking for a plot that has **Groups of patterns**
:::



## Not looking for...

:::{.large}
**Residuals correlated with predicted values**
:::

```{r}
#| purl: false
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 60%
set.seed(12346)
df <- tibble(
  fake_predicted = seq(0.2, 200, 0.2),
  fake_resid = fake_predicted + rnorm(1000, mean = 0, sd = 50)
)
ggplot(df, mapping = aes(x = fake_predicted, y = fake_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted (y_hat)", y = "Residuals (e)")
```


::: notes
- We also don't want Residuals to be correlated with predicted values
:::



## Not looking for...

:::{.large}
**Any patterns!**
:::

```{r}
#| purl: false
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 60%
set.seed(12346)
df <- tibble(
  fake_predicted = seq(-10, 10, 0.4),
  fake_resid = -.5*fake_predicted^3 - 3*fake_predicted + rnorm(length(fake_predicted), mean = 0, sd = 100)
)
ggplot(df, mapping = aes(x = fake_predicted, y = fake_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted (y_hat)", y = "Residuals (e)")
```

::: notes
- We basically don't want the residuals show Any patterns!
- If $X$ and $Y$ are not linearly related, or the residual plot exists some pattern, some data transformation is needed. Or use another model.
:::

# Considerations in the Usage of Regression



## Considerations in Regression: Extrapolation

- Regression models are most reliable for **interpolation** within *the range of predictor values* used to fit the model.


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
set.seed(9274)
x <- seq(-3, 4, 0.05)
y_s <-  -0.5 * x ^ 3 + x ^ 2 + x + rnorm(length(x), mean = 0, sd = 2)
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(y_s[1:40] ~ x[1:40], xlab = "", ylab = "", ylim = range(y_s), xlim = range(x),
     yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", pch = 19, col = "green3")
abline(lm(y_s[1:40] ~ x[1:40]), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
# abline(v = x[40], lty = 2, col = "red")
segments(x0 = -3, y0 = min(y_s)-0.5, x1 = x[40], y1 = min(y_s)-0.5, col = 2, 
         lwd = 3)
text(x = -2, y = min(y_s)+0.2, "range of x", cex = 1.5)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
set.seed(9274)
x <- seq(-3, 4, 0.05)
y_s <-  -0.5 * x ^ 3 + x ^ 2 + x + rnorm(length(x), mean = 0, sd = 2)
y_s_1 <- x ^ 2 + x + rnorm(length(x), mean = 0, sd = 2)
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(y_s ~ x, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", pch = 19, col = "green3")
points(y_s[41:length(x)] ~ x[41:length(x)], pch = 19, col = 1)
points(y_s_1[41:length(x)] ~ x[41:length(x)], pch = 19, col = 2)
abline(lm(y_s[1:40] ~ x[1:40]), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(v = x[40], lty = 2, col = "red")
# segments(x0 = -3, y0 = min(y_s)-0.5, x1 = x[40], y1 = min(y_s)-0.5, col = 2, 
#          lwd = 3)
# text(x = -2, y = min(y_s), "range of x")
```

:::

::::



::: notes

- First, Regression models are intended as **interpolation** equations over the range of the regressors used to fit the model.
- Regression does a really bad job for extrapolation. 
- Look at this figure for example.
- Suppose the data we collected have the range of X like this.
- Based on the data, we train our model, and estimate the parameters for prediction and inference.
- Our prediction and inference will be more plausible or convicing when the new $x$ is within the range of $X$.
- Again, the only information we have is our data. 
- When we do extrapolation, it's like doing a prediction or inference without any reliable information at hand.
- Our conclusion may be totally wrong. Based on the collected data, we thought x and y are linear related.
- But the true x-y relationship may not be linear at all, and because our data only cover a small range of $X$, we don't know what really happens outside the range of data. 
- We cannot say much about the predictive mean response or observation outside the range of $X$, and we cannot conclude the relationship between x and y outside the range as well.

:::


## Considerations in the Use of Regression: Outliers

- **Outlier**: An observation with an *unusual response value* relative to other observations, especially given its $x$ value.


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
set.seed(83629)
x <- seq(1, 30, 1)
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
y <- -2 * x + 20 + rnorm(length(x), mean = 0, sd = 10)
y_outlier <- c(y[1:15], y[16]+200, y[17:30])
plot(y_outlier ~ x, pch = 19, col = "black", 
     xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n")
lm_outlier = lm(y_outlier ~ x)
lm_no_outlier <- lm(y ~ x)
abline(lm_outlier, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(lm_no_outlier, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

:::



::: {.column width="50%"}

- The estimated coefficients may change substantially.

- The residual mean square may be inflated.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
summary(lm_outlier)$sigma ^ 2
summary(lm_no_outlier)$sigma ^ 2
```

:::

::::



::: notes

- The second consideration is outlier.
- it might be just measurement error.
- If it is not an typo, we have to look into this point with great care, and see why this happened and see if we need to do some correction to it.
- We will talk about outliers in detail later in this course.

:::



## Considerations in Regression: Influential Points {.nostretch}

- **Influential point**: An observation whose inclusion substantially *changes the fitted regression results*; it often has an *unusual $x$ value.*

```{r}
#| out-width: 65%
x_influential <- c(x[1:29], 200)
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(y ~ x_influential, pch = 19, col = "black", 
     xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n")
lm_influential = lm(y ~ x_influential)
lm_influential_rm <- lm(y ~ x)
abline(lm_influential, col = "blue")
abline(lm_influential_rm, col = "red")
```


::: notes

- Our inference and prediction may be totally distorted just because of one single influential point. So again, we have to very careful about it.

:::


## Considerations in Regression: Causal Interpretation?
<!-- - Correlation is NOT Causation! -->
<!-- - Remember this when interpreting model coefficients! -->

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| out-width: 56%
knitr::include_graphics("./images/04-slr-f26/icecream.jpeg")
```

```{r}
#| out-width: 90%
par(mar = c(3, 3, 0, 0), mgp = c(2, 0.5, 0))
drowning <- c(2, 3, 7, 9, 14, 27, 33, 38, 28, 13, 7, 2)
ice_cream <- drowning + rnorm(12, 0, 3)
plot(1:12, drowning, axes = F, xlab = "", type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 3, ylab = "")
axis(1, at = 1:12, labels = month.abb, cex.axis = 0.8)
axis(2, tick = FALSE, labels = FALSE)
lines(ice_cream, col = "blue", lwd = 3)
legend("topleft", c("Ice Cream Sales", "Drownings"), col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = c(3, 3), bty = "n")
```

:::



::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| out-width: 56%
knitr::include_graphics("./images/04-slr-f26/drowning.jpeg")
```

```{r}
#| out-width: 90%
par(mar = c(3, 3, 0.1, 0.1), mgp = c(2, 0.5, 0))
drowning <- sort(as.integer(runif(40, 0, 40)))
ice_cream_sale <- sort(as.integer(runif(40, 10, 35)))
plot(ice_cream_sale, drowning, las = 1,
     xlab = "Drownings", ylab = "Ice Cream Sales (thousands $)")
abline(lm(drowning~ice_cream_sale)$coef, col = "red", lwd  = 2)
```

:::

::::

::: notes

- Regression is just a model. It does not tell you X-Y's relationship is correlation relationship or causal relationship. 
- It is the person who uses the model tell the relationship.
- So we have to be careful when interpreting regression result.
- They are correlated, not one causes the other.
- Actually, there is another factor that causes the sales and # of drownings to go up and down together.

:::


## Considerations in Regression: Unknown Predictor

- Consider maximum daily electrical load $(Y)$ and maximum daily temperature $(X)$.

- To predict tomorrow's maximum load, we must first know or forecast tomorrow's maximum temperature.

- The load prediction is therefore **conditional** on the temperature forecast.


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("./images/04-slr-f26/electricity.jpeg")
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("./images/04-slr-f26/electricity_snow.jpeg")
```

:::

::::



## Outlier, leverage, influence  {visibility="hidden"}

| Term | Plain meaning | Main question |
|---|---|---|
| Outlier | unusual $Y$ given its $X$ | does the model miss this case? |
| High leverage | unusual $X$ value | can this point pull the line? |
| Influential | changes the fitted result | does the conclusion depend on it? |



## Influence is about what changes  {visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: influence-plot
set.seed(481)
base_dat <- tibble(x = runif(35, 1, 6), y = 35 - 3 * x + rnorm(35, 0, 2.2))
infl_dat <- bind_rows(base_dat, tibble(x = 9.0, y = 34)) |>
  mutate(point_type = ifelse(row_number() == n(), "added point", "original data"))
fit_no <- lm(y ~ x, data = base_dat)
fit_yes <- lm(y ~ x, data = infl_dat)
line_infl <- tibble(x = seq(1, 9, length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(without_point = coef(fit_no)[1] + coef(fit_no)[2] * x,
         with_point = coef(fit_yes)[1] + coef(fit_yes)[2] * x) |>
  pivot_longer(-x, names_to = "fit", values_to = "y")

ggplot(infl_dat, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = point_type), size = 2.7, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(data = line_infl, aes(x, y, linetype = fit), linewidth = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "A high-leverage point can change the fitted line",
    x = "X",
    y = "Y",
    shape = NULL,
    linetype = NULL
  )
```



## Leave-one-out sensitivity  {visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: leave-one-out
loo_slopes <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(infl_dat)), function(i) {
  fit_i <- lm(y ~ x, data = infl_dat[-i, ])
  tibble(omitted = i, slope = coef(fit_i)[2], x = infl_dat$x[i], y = infl_dat$y[i])
}) |> bind_rows() |>
  mutate(point = ifelse(omitted == nrow(infl_dat), "added point", "other"))

ggplot(loo_slopes, aes(omitted, slope)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = coef(fit_yes)[2], linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = point), size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "If removing one point changes the slope, inspect it",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: slope using all observations",
    x = "Omitted observation index",
    y = "Slope after omitting that observation",
    shape = NULL
  )
```



## $R^2$: useful but limited  {visibility="hidden"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

```{r}
#| label: anscombe-r2
ans <- datasets::anscombe |>
  as_tibble()
ans_long <- bind_rows(
  tibble(set = "I", x = ans$x1, y = ans$y1),
  tibble(set = "II", x = ans$x2, y = ans$y2),
  tibble(set = "III", x = ans$x3, y = ans$y3),
  tibble(set = "IV", x = ans$x4, y = ans$y4)
)

ggplot(ans_long, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.0) +
  facet_wrap(~ set, nrow = 2) +
  labs(title = "Similar summaries, very different data", x = "X", y = "Y")
```

:::

::: {.column width="53%"}

| $R^2$ says | $R^2$ does not say |
|---|---|
| in-sample variance explained | causal validity |
| fit relative to mean-only model | linearity is adequate |
| descriptive strength | prediction works on new data |
| one-number summary | conclusions are robust |

:::

:::

# Interpretation and misuse  {visibility="hidden"}

## Association is not automatically causation  {visibility="hidden"}

| Regression output | Causal interpretation needs |
|---|---|
| slope of $Y$ on $X$ | a causal question |
| adjustment variables | pre-treatment covariates, not post-treatment variables |
| small p-value | not enough |
| good prediction | not enough |
| observational data | design and assumptions about confounding |



## Regression conclusion template  {visibility="hidden"}

> Among **[population]**, over **[range of X]**, a one-unit increase in **[X]** is associated with an estimated **[change]** in the conditional mean of **[Y]**. The uncertainty interval is **[interval]**. This is **[prediction / description / comparison / causal claim]**, and the main limitations are **[diagnostics / sampling / confounding / extrapolation]**.

## Checklist Before Reporting a Regression Analysis

| Check | Ask this before you report |
|---|---|
| Goal | prediction, description, comparison, or causality? |
| Scale | are units and transformations clear? |
| Range | interpolation or extrapolation? |
| Uncertainty | mean response or new observation? |
| Diagnostics | what pattern remains in residuals? |
| Sensitivity | do a few observations drive the result? |
| Causality | what design or assumptions justify causal language? |
